entities.name: Badshahi Mosque
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Badshahi Mosque (Emperor's Mosque) in Lahore, Pakistan is the world's second-largest mosque and one of the finest examples of Mughal architecture, built by Emperor Aurangzeb between 1671 and 1673 CE. The mosque's dramatic red sandstone construction with white marble inlay, four towering minarets (each 54 meters high), and an octagonal forecourt accommodating 100,000 worshippers creates one of the most visually striking religious monuments in Asia.

Aurangzeb, the last of the great Mughal emperors, built the Badshahi Mosque directly facing the Lahore Fort across the Hazuri Bagh garden, creating the most magnificent ceremonial ensemble in Mughal architecture. The prayer hall's marble interior contains black marble pedestals and traces of original mirrorwork; the forecourt is large enough to accommodate 100,000 worshippers during Eid prayers — more than any other mosque at the time of its construction.

The mosque's history reflects South Asian turmoil: during Sikh rule (1799-1849), Maharaja Ranjit Singh stabled horses in the prayer hall; the British used it as a garrison and powder magazine until 1856. Pakistani independence in 1947 restored the mosque to Muslim use, and extensive restoration through the 1960s-1970s repaired colonial damage. The mosque houses relics including alleged strands of the Prophet Muhammad's beard, his mantle, and sandals, making it a major pilgrimage destination. The Badshahi Mosque is on Pakistan's Rs.10 banknote.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Badshahi Mosque is the culminating achievement of Mughal mosque architecture, its 100,000-person capacity forecourt making it Asia's grandest congregational space and a symbol of the Mughal Empire's magnificent final flowering.
